newsitem.title: USA: Jurors begin weighing punitive damages on Simpson.
newsitem.headline: Jurors begin weighing punitive damages on Simpson.

text.p: Jurors in the O.J. Simpson civil trial began deliberations on Friday on whether the former football star should be forced to pay punitive damages in the deaths of his ex-wife and her friend.
The jury entered the final decisive phase of the four-month trial three days after blaming Simpson for the murders and ordering him to pay $8.5 million in compensatory damages.

In an impassioned closing argument, Daniel Petrocelli, the plaintiffs' lead attorney, urged jurors to impose stiff punitive damages and declare to the world that "You cannot kill two people and get away with it."
Accusing Simpson of cowardice for failing to show up in court on Friday, Petrocelli implored jurors to "send him a message so loud that he can hear it on whatever golf course he's hiding out on."
But lead defence attorney Robert Baker contended that "Mr. Simpson has already been punished by the $8.5 million award" and said anything more would effectively "destroy" his client.
Simpson was cleared of murder charges in October 1995 but the victims' families pressed ahead with a wrongful-death lawsuit in civil court.

Petrocelli, in an emotional final summation, told jurors: "You are the last ones who will have the power to punish Mr Simpson for killing two people and walking away from it scot-free. I leave it to you to decide what is just."
"He can't come in here and face you, ladies and gentlemen, because you are the truth and you have declared that he is a killer," Petrocelli added.

The jury on Tuesday blamed Simpson for the June 12, 1994, murders of his ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and her friend, Ronald Goldman, and awarded $8.5 million in damages to Goldman's divorced parents.

The plaintiffs now want the jury to punish him further by awarding millions more to the estates of Nicole Brown Simpson and Goldman. Simpson was cleared of murder charges in October 1995 but the victims' families pressed ahead with a wrongful-death lawsuit in civil court.

As the trial neared its conclusion, Brown family attorney John Kelly made the day's only reference to a specific dollar amount for punitive damages, reminding jurors that Simpson had pledged in 1989 to pay Nicole Brown Simpson between $5 million and $6 million if he even hit her again.

Petrocelli, who represents the Goldman family, looked directly into the eyes of the jury and in a loud, booming voice, declared: "You must send him a message that ... you cannot kill two people and get away with it no matter how much money you have, no matter how many lies you tell."

He told the jury that while they cannot send Simpson to prison, they had the power to exact a severe price. "He will get to enjoy the rest of his life as a free man while his victims lie in their graves," Petrocelli said. Any punitive damages for the death of Goldman would go to his divorced parents.

Referring to testimony by a plaintiffs' expert that Simpson could make millions of dollars by cashing in on his notoriety, he said: "Make him pay, ladies and gentlemen. Don't let him dismiss away your verdict by signing a few more autographs."

Kelly asked the jurors to remember that any punitive damages awarded to Nicole Brown Simpson's estate would flow to her heirs -- the two young children she had with her celebrity husband -- and that Simpson would not be able to touch the money.

Earlier in the session, jurors were told Simpson was unable to earn any money and was struggling to pay his bills. Leroy "Skip" Taft, Simpson's business manager, said Simpson's current earning capacity was nil and his future prospects were bleak.
Taft, a defence witness, gave the jurors a glimpse of what it costs to live in the world of the rich and famous, listing Simpson's considerable monthly expenses.
He said the mortgage on Simpson's mansion in the posh Brentwood section of Los Angeles was $24,000 and month "when he pays it," and the cost of maintaining the estate was about $30,000 a month.
